contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you learned faster objects have more energy. Today, what happens to that energy the moment two objects actually collide?

When two objects collide, energy transfers between them — the moving object's energy causes a change in the object (or objects) it hits. Think through these predictions before testing them: if a marble rolls into a line of dominoes, what happens to the dominoes? If two balls of the same size collide head-on at the same speed, what happens to each one? If a fast-moving ball hits a much heavier, still object, does the heavy object move as far as a light object would? Test at least one of these predictions with real objects at home, and compare what actually happened to your prediction.
You just predicted and tested what happens when moving objects collide — real evidence of energy transferring on impact. Tomorrow we'll look at devices that convert energy from one form into another.

objectives: Ask questions and make predictions about the effects of a collision between moving objects
Test a collision prediction against real evidence and compare
materialsNeeded: A second ball of similar size (optional)
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review Day 2's speed-energy connection.
2. Walk through the 3 collision scenarios as predictions before testing anything.
3. Test at least one scenario for real, comparing the actual outcome to the prediction.
4. Discuss why a heavier, still object moves less than a light one when hit with the same energy.
5. Complete the worksheet.
6. Preview tomorrow's topic: energy-converting devices.
differentiationTips: Struggling: focus on just the marble-and-dominoes scenario, the most visually clear collision example
Ready for more: test the heavy-vs-light object scenario and measure roughly how far each one moved
Encourage genuine prediction-then-test, not just testing directly — the prediction step is where the real thinking happens
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. A marble hitting a line of dominoes causes them to fall in sequence — energy transfers from domino to domino. 2. Two equal balls colliding head-on at equal speed generally stop or bounce back, transferring energy between them. 3. A heavy, still object hit by a fast light object moves less far than a light, still object would, because more of its mass resists the same amount of energy.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses NGSS 4-PS3-3: asking questions and predicting outcomes about changes in energy that occur when objects collide.

generationData.instructions: For each scenario, write your prediction, then what actually happened when you tested it.
